## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Session 1: declared the design, saw why weights matter
- Today: the **survey versions** of the descriptive tools you already know
- By the end you can:
  - estimate **means, proportions, totals and quantiles** with CIs
  - estimate by **groups**
  - read a **design effect**
  - do a **subpopulation** analysis correctly
  - test an association in a **weighted table**
:::

# Topic 1 — Means, proportions, totals {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Means and totals

```{r}
m <- svymean(~sbp, des); m; confint(m)
svytotal(~hypertension, des)
```

::: {.key}
Mean SBP **125.7 mmHg** (95% CI 124.6 to 126.9). About **82,700 adults** in the population have hypertension (SE 6,000): a **total** needs the weights, since it scales up to the population.
:::

## A proportion with a good CI

```{r}
svyciprop(~I(hypertension == 1), des, method = "logit")
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Logit** (or Wilson-type) intervals stay between 0 and 1 and behave better for small or large proportions
- **20.0%**, 95% CI **17.1% to 23.1%**
- Note the **`I(... == 1)`**: `svyciprop` needs a logical or 0/1 formula
:::

## By groups

```{r}
svyby(~hypertension, ~residence, des, svymean)
```

```{r}
svyby(~hypertension, ~region, des, svymean, vartype = c("se", "ci"))
```

::: {.key}
**Urban 29.7%** vs **rural 16.1%**. Regions look alike (19 to 23%); the CIs are wide because each region has only **12 PSUs**.
:::

## Quantiles

```{r}
svyquantile(~sbp, des, quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
```

::: {.incremental}
- `median()` and `quantile()` **ignore the weights**: they describe the **sample**
- `svyquantile()` gives the **population** quartiles with CIs: median **126 mmHg**
:::

# Topic 2 — Design effect and subpopulations {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Design effect

```{r}
svymean(~hypertension, des, deff = TRUE)
```

::: {.eq}
DEFF = variance (actual design) / variance (simple random sample of the same size)       n~eff~ = n / DEFF
:::

::: {.incremental}
- DEFF **2.6**: the 1,853 respondents carry the information of about **710** independent adults
- Comes from **clustering** (similar adults in a PSU) and **unequal weights**
- **Differs by outcome**: large when the outcome varies a lot between PSUs
:::

## Subpopulations

```{r}
des_w30 <- subset(des, sex == "Female" & age >= 30)
svymean(~hypertension, des_w30)
```

::: {.warn}
Use **`subset()` on the design**, not `filter()` on the data followed by a new `svydesign()`. `subset()` keeps the **whole design** (all strata and PSUs), so the variance is right. Filtering can remove a PSU from a stratum and make the variance **wrong** or impossible.
:::

## Weighted tables and tests

```{r}
svytable(~education + hypertension, des) |> round(0)
svychisq(~education + hypertension, des)
```

::: {.incremental}
- Counts are **estimated numbers of adults**, not respondents
- About **21% and 22%** (none, primary) vs **17%** (secondary or more)
- **Rao-Scott** test (p ≈ 0.05); never `chisq.test()` on survey data
:::

## The same with srvyr (tidy syntax)

```{r}
resp |> as_survey_design(ids = psu, strata = stratum, weights = weight, nest = TRUE) |> group_by(residence) |>
  summarise(prev = survey_mean(hypertension, vartype = "ci"), n = unweighted(n()))
```

::: {.key}
`survey_mean()`, `survey_total()`, `survey_quantile()` plug into `group_by()` and `summarise()`; `unweighted(n())` gives the **respondent** count.
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("v2q1", "Why is the logit method often chosen for the CI of a prevalence?",
         c("It makes the interval narrower than a symmetric one around the estimate",
           "It removes the design effect from the standard error of the proportion",
           "It is the only method that works when weights are present",
           "It keeps the interval between 0 and 1 and suits small proportions"), answer = 4,
         explain = "A symmetric interval can fall below 0 or above 1 for proportions near the ends. The logit scale keeps limits inside the range.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("v2q2", "Why use subset() on the design instead of filtering the data and declaring the design again?",
         c("The full design is kept, so the variance reflects all strata and PSUs",
           "Filtering rescales the weights so that they add up to the sample size",
           "subset() is quicker because it does not need to look at the strata",
           "Filtering removes the variable that identifies the strata from the data"), answer = 1,
         explain = "Subpopulation estimates must use the complete design. Removing rows can drop PSUs and change the variance, sometimes leaving strata with a single PSU.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("v2q3", "The design effect for hypertension is 2.6 and n is 1,853. What is the effective sample size?",
         c("About 4,800 respondents",
           "About 1,850 respondents",
           "About 710 respondents",
           "About 70 respondents"), answer = 3,
         explain = "The effective sample size is n divided by the design effect: 1,853 / 2.6 is about 710.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("v2q4", "svytotal(~hypertension, des) gives 82,700. What does this estimate?",
         c("The number of respondents in the sample who have hypertension",
           "The number of adults in the population who have hypertension",
           "The mean blood pressure of the adults who have hypertension",
           "The number of PSUs in which hypertension was recorded"), answer = 2,
         explain = "A total is the weighted sum: each respondent counts for the number of adults he or she represents, giving a population count.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("v2q5", "Why should svyquantile() be used rather than median() for the median SBP of the population?",
         c("median() cannot handle missing values in the blood pressure column",
           "svyquantile() is for percentages while median() is for means",
           "median() ignores the weights, so it describes the sample",
           "median() needs the data to be sorted by stratum before it is called"), answer = 3,
         explain = "The ordinary median treats every respondent equally. The survey version applies the weights, so it estimates the population median.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- `svymean`, `svytotal`, `svyciprop(method = "logit")`, `svyquantile`, `svyby`
- **DEFF** = variance ratio; **n~eff~ = n / DEFF**
- **`subset(design)`**, never filter then re-declare
- `svytable` + **Rao-Scott** (`svychisq`), not `chisq.test()`
- srvyr: `as_survey_design()` + `survey_mean()`
:::
